entry.sum: Differentiation and integration undo each other. If $f$ is continuous, the accumulated area $F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt$ has derivative $f(x)$; and if $G$ is any antiderivative of an integrable $f$, then $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = G(b) - G(a)$.
entry.why: It replaces the limit of sums that defines an integral by the far easier task of finding an antiderivative, and it is why the total change of a quantity can be computed from its rate of change.

links.note: Displacement is the integral of velocity and the work done equals the change in kinetic energy, both instances of integrating a derivative.
Solving y' = f(x), and separable equations more generally, is integration made possible by the theorem.
A distribution function is the integral of its density, so by the first form of the theorem the density is the derivative of the distribution function at every point where the density is continuous.

refs: Courant & John, Introduction to Calculus and Analysis I

blocks.body:
In [[riemann-integral]] it took a page of algebra and a formula for $\sum i^3$ to show that $\int_0^b x^3\,dx = \frac{b^4}{4}$. For $x^{10}$, or $\sin x$, or $\frac{1}{1 + x^2}$, the same method would be hopeless. Yet Newton and Leibniz computed such integrals in a line, because they had noticed something remarkable: the answer $\frac{b^4}{4}$ is a function of $b$ whose derivative is $b^3$, the integrand.

The fundamental theorem of calculus explains why. It says that integration and differentiation undo each other: the rate at which accumulated area grows is the height of the curve, and an integral can be evaluated by finding any function whose derivative is the integrand. This lesson states both halves carefully and proves them, using [[mvt]] for the second.

blocks.title: The area function
blocks.body:
Fix $f$ on $[a, b]$ and let $F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt$ be the area accumulated from $a$ up to $x$. How fast does $F$ grow? Moving from $x$ to $x + h$ adds a thin strip of width $h$ whose height is close to $f(x)$, so
$$F(x + h) - F(x) = \int_x^{x+h}f(t)\,dt \approx f(x)\,h, \qquad \frac{F(x + h) - F(x)}{h} \approx f(x).$$
For $f(t) = t^2$ and $a = 0$ we know that $F(x) = \frac{x^3}{3}$. At $x = 1$ the difference quotients are
$$\frac{(1 + h)^3 - 1}{3h} = 1 + h + \frac{h^2}{3},$$
which equals $1.10333\ldots$ for $h = 0.1$ and $1.0100333\ldots$ for $h = 0.01$, approaching $f(1) = 1$. The first form of the theorem makes the "$\approx$" exact for continuous $f$.

blocks.title: Fundamental theorem of calculus, first form
blocks.body:
Let $f$ be integrable on $[a, b]$ and define $F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt$ for $a \le x \le b$. Then $F$ is continuous on $[a, b]$. If moreover $f$ is continuous at a point $c \in (a, b)$, then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$$F'(c) = f(c).$$
In particular, if $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, then $\dfrac{d}{dx}\displaystyle\int_a^x f(t)\,dt = f(x)$ for every $x \in (a, b)$.

An integrable function is bounded by definition, say $|f| \le M$. For $a \le x < y \le b$, additivity gives $F(y) - F(x) = \int_x^y f$, and monotonicity gives $\left|\int_x^y f\right| \le M(y - x)$. So $|F(y) - F(x)| \le M|y - x|$, and $F$ is continuous.

Now let $f$ be continuous at $c$, and let $\varepsilon > 0$. Choose $\delta > 0$ such that $|f(t) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ for all $t \in [a, b]$ with $|t - c| < \delta$. For $0 < h < \delta$ with $c + h \le b$, using $\int_c^{c+h}f(c)\,dt = f(c)\,h$,
$$\frac{F(c + h) - F(c)}{h} - f(c) = \frac1h\int_c^{c+h}f(t)\,dt - \frac1h\int_c^{c+h}f(c)\,dt = \frac1h\int_c^{c+h}\big(f(t) - f(c)\big)\,dt.$$
The integrand has absolute value less than $\varepsilon$, so the right side has absolute value at most $\frac1h\cdot\varepsilon h = \varepsilon$. For $-\delta < h < 0$ with $c + h \ge a$, the same computation with $\frac{1}{|h|}\int_{c+h}^{c}$ gives the same bound. Hence the difference quotient tends to $f(c)$.

blocks.title: Antiderivative
blocks.body:
Let $f$ be defined on an interval $I$. A function $G$ is an antiderivative (or primitive) of $f$ on $I$ if $G'(x) = f(x)$ for every $x \in I$. The family of all antiderivatives is written $\int f(x)\,dx = G(x) + C$ and called the indefinite integral; we also write $\big[G(x)\big]_a^b = G(b) - G(a)$.

If $G$ is one antiderivative on an interval, every other one is $G + C$ for a constant $C$, because the difference has derivative $0$ and is therefore constant by [[mvt]].

blocks.title: Fundamental theorem of calculus, second form
blocks.body:
Let $G$ be continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$, and suppose $G'(x) = f(x)$ for $a < x < b$, where $f$ is integrable on $[a, b]$. Then
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = G(b) - G(a).$$

Take any partition $a = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_n = b$. On each piece $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$ the mean value theorem gives a point $c_i \in (x_{i-1}, x_i)$ with
$$G(x_i) - G(x_{i-1}) = G'(c_i)\,\Delta x_i = f(c_i)\,\Delta x_i.$$
Adding these $n$ equations, the left side telescopes:
$$G(b) - G(a) = \sum_{i=1}^n f(c_i)\,\Delta x_i.$$
The right side is a Riemann sum for this partition $P$, so it lies between $L(f, P)$ and $U(f, P)$. Thus the single number $G(b) - G(a)$ lies between every lower sum and every upper sum, that is, $\sup_P L(f, P) \le G(b) - G(a) \le \inf_P U(f, P)$. Since $f$ is integrable, both ends equal $\int_a^b f$.

blocks.title: Using the theorem
blocks.body:
The second form reduces evaluating an integral to finding an antiderivative. Reading the rules of [[diff-rules]] backwards gives a first table, valid on any interval where the formulas make sense:
$$\int x^r\,dx = \frac{x^{r+1}}{r + 1} + C \ \ (r \ne -1), \qquad \int\frac{dx}{x} = \ln|x| + C, \qquad \int e^x\,dx = e^x + C,$$
$$\int\sin x\,dx = -\cos x + C, \qquad \int\cos x\,dx = \sin x + C, \qquad \int\frac{dx}{1 + x^2} = \arctan x + C.$$
Now the parabola area from [[riemann-integral]] takes one line: $\int_0^1 x^2\,dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = \frac13$. The area under one arch of the sine curve is $\int_0^\pi\sin x\,dx = \big[-\cos x\big]_0^\pi = 1 - (-1) = 2$.

The first form, in turn, guarantees that every continuous function on an interval has an antiderivative, namely $x \mapsto \int_a^x f$, even when no formula for it exists. For instance $\int_0^x e^{-t^2}\,dt$ is a perfectly good differentiable function with derivative $e^{-x^2}$, though it cannot be written in terms of elementary functions. The normal distribution function of probability is built from it: $\Phi(x) = \frac12 + \frac{1}{\sqrt\pi}\int_0^{x/\sqrt2}e^{-t^2}\,dt$.

Physically, if $s(t)$ is the position of a particle and $v(t) = s'(t)$ its velocity, the displacement between times $t_0$ and $t_1$ is $\int_{t_0}^{t_1}v(t)\,dt = s(t_1) - s(t_0)$. The total change of a quantity is the integral of its rate of change.

blocks.title: Evaluating integrals
blocks.body: Compute (a) $\displaystyle\int_1^4\left(\sqrt x + \frac{1}{x^2}\right)dx$; (b) the area of the region between the graphs of $y = x$ and $y = x^2$.
blocks.solution:
(a) An antiderivative of $x^{1/2} + x^{-2}$ on $[1, 4]$ is $\frac23x^{3/2} - x^{-1}$. So the integral is
$$\left(\frac23\cdot 8 - \frac14\right) - \left(\frac23 - 1\right) = \frac{16}{3} - \frac14 - \frac23 + 1 = \frac{65}{12}.$$

(b) The graphs meet where $x = x^2$, at $x = 0$ and $x = 1$, and between these points $x \ge x^2$. The area is the integral of the upper function minus the lower one:
$$\int_0^1(x - x^2)\,dx = \left[\frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = \frac12 - \frac13 = \frac16.$$

blocks.title: Differentiating an integral
blocks.body: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\displaystyle\int_x^{2x}e^{-t^2}\,dt$ and $\dfrac{d}{dx}\displaystyle\int_0^{x^2}\sin(t^2)\,dt$.
blocks.solution:
Let $E(u) = \int_0^u e^{-t^2}\,dt$. By the first form, $E'(u) = e^{-u^2}$. By additivity, $\int_x^{2x}e^{-t^2}\,dt = E(2x) - E(x)$, and the chain rule gives
$$\frac{d}{dx}\big(E(2x) - E(x)\big) = 2e^{-4x^2} - e^{-x^2}.$$
Likewise, with $S(u) = \int_0^u\sin(t^2)\,dt$, the second function is $S(x^2)$, and its derivative is $S'(x^2)\cdot 2x = 2x\sin(x^4)$.

In general, for continuous $f$ and differentiable $u$ and $v$,
$$\frac{d}{dx}\int_{v(x)}^{u(x)}f(t)\,dt = f(u(x))\,u'(x) - f(v(x))\,v'(x).$$
Neither integral has a closed form in elementary functions, but their derivatives are easy.

blocks.title: A sum that becomes ln 2
blocks.body: Find $\displaystyle\lim_{n \to \infty}\left(\frac{1}{n + 1} + \frac{1}{n + 2} + \dots + \frac{1}{2n}\right)$.
blocks.solution:
Write the $k$-th term as $\frac1n\cdot\dfrac{1}{1 + k/n}$ for $k = 1, \dots, n$. The sum is then the right-endpoint Riemann sum, with $n$ equal pieces, for $f(x) = \frac{1}{1 + x}$ on $[0, 1]$. As $f$ is continuous, the sums converge to
$$\int_0^1\frac{dx}{1 + x} = \big[\ln(1 + x)\big]_0^1 = \ln 2.$$
Numerically, the sum is $0.6906\ldots$ for $n = 100$, against $\ln 2 = 0.6931\ldots$.

blocks.title: An integral equation
blocks.body:
Find all continuous functions $f : \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ such that
$$f(x) = 1 + \int_0^x f(t)\,dt \quad \text{for all real } x.$$
blocks.solution:
Since $f$ is continuous, the right side is differentiable by the first form, so $f$ itself is differentiable, with
$$f'(x) = f(x) \quad\text{for all } x, \qquad f(0) = 1 + \int_0^0 f = 1.$$
Let $g(x) = e^{-x}f(x)$. Then $g'(x) = e^{-x}\big(f'(x) - f(x)\big) = 0$, so $g$ is constant by [[mvt]], and $g(0) = 1$. Hence $f(x) = e^x$. Conversely, $1 + \int_0^x e^t\,dt = 1 + (e^x - 1) = e^x$, so $f(x) = e^x$ is the unique solution.

The pattern here, using the first form to turn an equation involving integrals into a differential equation, is a starting point of [[ode-first]].

blocks.body:
- The second form needs an integrable $f$. The "computation" $\int_{-1}^1\frac{dx}{x^2} = \left[-\frac1x\right]_{-1}^1 = -2$ is nonsense: a positive function cannot have a negative integral. Here $\frac{1}{x^2}$ is unbounded near $0$, and $-\frac1x$ is not an antiderivative on any interval containing $0$.
- The first form needs continuity at the point. If $f = -1$ on $[-1, 0)$ and $f = 1$ on $[0, 1]$, then $F(x) = \int_0^x f(t)\,dt = |x|$, which is not differentiable at $0$.
- Antiderivatives are unique up to a constant only on an interval. On $\mathbb R \setminus \{0\}$, the function equal to $\ln|x| + C_1$ for $x > 0$ and $\ln|x| + C_2$ for $x < 0$ is an antiderivative of $\frac1x$ for any two constants.
- Keep the variables apart: in $\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$ the integration variable is $t$. Writing $\int_a^x f(x)\,dx$ invites errors.
- A derivative need not be integrable. $G(x) = x^2\sin(1/x^2)$ with $G(0) = 0$ is differentiable everywhere, but $G'$ is unbounded near $0$, so $G'$ is not Riemann integrable on $[0, 1]$ and the second form does not apply to it.

Reading the differentiation rules backwards through the second form gives [[integration-techniques]]: the chain rule becomes substitution and the product rule becomes integration by parts. Combined with limits, the theorem evaluates [[improper-integrals]]. In several variables, iterated integrals are computed one variable at a time with it ([[multiple-integrals]]), and it generalises to the theorems of Green, Stokes and Gauss, which say that integrating a derivative over a region equals integrating the function over the boundary ([[vector-calculus]]).

Solving $y' = f(x)$ is integration, and separable equations reduce to two integrals ([[ode-first]]). In probability, a distribution function is the integral of its density, so the density is its derivative at every point where the density is continuous ([[distributions]]). Starting from $f(x) = f(a) + \int_a^x f'(t)\,dt$ and integrating by parts repeatedly gives the integral form of the remainder in [[taylor]]. For integrals along a smooth curve $\gamma$ in the complex plane, parametrised by $[0, 1]$, the second form still holds, $\int_\gamma F'(z)\,dz = F(\gamma(1)) - F(\gamma(0))$; so a function with an antiderivative integrates to $0$ around every closed curve, and Cauchy's theorem for [[holomorphic]] functions shows that on a disc every holomorphic function has an antiderivative.
